newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope excommunicates renegade Sri Lankan priest.
newsitem.headline: Pope excommunicates renegade Sri Lankan priest.

text.p: Renegade Sri Lankan priest Tissa Balasuriya has been excommunicated for challenging fundamental beliefs of the Roman Catholic Church, the Vatican said.

Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, said in an official statement dated Saturday that the penalty was incurred over a "a series of grave errors" in the cleric's vision which distorted Catholic dogma.

Balasuriya refused to retract claims made in his book "Mary and Human Liberation", published by his Centre for Society and Religion, in which he questioned fundamental Catholic beliefs like baptism, original sin and the immaculate conception.
"Father Balasuriya has deviated from the integrity of the truth of the Catholic faith and therefore cannot be considered a Catholic theologian," Ratzinger's statement said.
"Moreover, he has incurred excommunication latae sententiae," he added in the statement, dated Saturday.
Excommunication -- which forbids excommunicates to receive the sacraments or share in acts of public worship -- is usually imposed "ferendae sententiae", that is after a formal "trial".

However seven offences, including heresy, schism, laying violent hands on the Pope and procuring abortion, are considered so disruptive of ecclesiastical life that they trigger automatic excommunication "latae sententiae". It is very rare.
Father Balasuriya told Reuters in Colombo he could not comment until he was officially notified. Church officials said they believed it was the first time a Sri Lankan priest had been excommunicated.
The Roman Catholic Church first denounced Balasuriya's book in 1994 and ordered him to stop reading from it. He refused.

Balasuriya last month refused to sign a Profession of Faith, especially drafted for him by the Church, saying it was not in line with current theological thinking and that his conscience would not allow him to sign.

He appealed directly to Pope John Paul, saying his text was within the limits of orthodoxy. The appeal for a stay of excommunication fell on deaf ears after the Vatican said Balasuriya refused to adhere to the faith of the Church.
